paragraphs: You already speak English all day, and this course asks you to look at it the way a maker looks at a tool. Writers study how sentences are built because a well-built sentence can be checked: you can find who acts, you can see where the verb sits, and you can spot the words that do nothing. Critics study speeches, poems and stories for a similar reason. Once you can name the parts, you can say why a line moves you or why a paragraph falls flat.

The course has twelve lessons in four parts. The sentence takes sentences apart into clauses, joins them with the right marks and puts actors back where readers expect them. Argument and rhetoric looks at how an argument is built and how famous speakers persuaded. Reading poetry covers metre, sound and the sonnet. Reading prose and drama looks at point of view, irony and the shape of a plot.
Each lesson explains first and asks afterwards, so you meet a question only once you have been shown what it needs. School terms are explained where they first appear.
outcomes: You'll be able to find the verb and its subject in a line of verse, even when the words are shuffled.
You'll be able to join two clauses with the mark that says what you mean.
You'll be able to rewrite a passive or padded sentence so that the actor leads and every word counts.
You'll be able to split an argument into claim, grounds and warrant, and say where it can be attacked.
You'll be able to scan a line of pentameter and say who is telling a story and how far to trust them.
prerequisites: You should read English comfortably; no grammar or literary training is assumed.
